title: Frida
full_review:
Salma Hayek gives a feisty performance in the title role of "Frida" (Miramax), a glossy dramatization about Mexican folk artist Frida Kahlo, who lived a short but passionate life of politics, sex and art.

A 1925 bus crash left the rebellious 18-year-old horribly injured after a metal rod pierced her hip, exited her groin, and portions of her skeleton were shattered. Though Frida is bedridden in a body cast, her parents encouraged her artistic talent, designing an easel and mirror positioned above her so she could paint -- with herself as a model. Frida had begun a lifetime of pouring her physical and then emotional pain into her vivid, surrealistic art in which she was often the subject of the canvas.

The movie, however, focuses just as much on her volatile relationship with famed muralist Diego Rivera (Alfred Molina in fine form), the mentor she married in 1929 despite her Catholic mother's protest (after reminding her mother that she herself chose to marry a Jewish man). Her mother objected to the 21-year age difference, Diego's atheism and his scandalous reputation.

Diego had inspired Frida's artistic ambitions, shared her left-wing politics and divorced his wife (Valeria Golino) to marry her. He also made it clear she would have his loyalty but not his fidelity, as he had no intention of reining in his womanizing ways. Intellectually, Frida accepts this nonsense about loyalty but soon jealousy and rage well up and she begins having casual affairs with both men and women. In spite of being devastated by her husband's promiscuity, she chooses to inflict the same hurt on the man she loves the most.

As directed by Julie Taymor, the film celebrates Frida's life's struggle without judging her promiscuity or bisexuality. This is troubling, yet what clearly emerges is how harmful marital infidelity was to both Frida and Diego. This is most apparent when Frida discovers Diego and her own beloved sister (Mia Maestro) are sleeping together, rupturing their close sibling relationship and bringing more pain to all three. However, through all the recriminations and separations (including a divorce and remarriage to each other) the two came to realize theirs was an enduring connection that ultimately led to unconditional love. In showing the unhappy consequences of adultery, the movie offers a cautionary note and suggests that the old chestnut that artists are not bound by traditional morality doesn't mean they won't suffer as a result.

Taymor, who brought "The Lion King" to Broadway, uses creative filmmaking techniques to incorporate Kahlo's paintings into the narrative, using animation and even puppetry in an impressive command of cinematic language. She directs with a flair for theatricality and spectacle in vivid colors that reflect Kahlo's preferred palette. The paintings shown convey Kahlo's very personal, primitive and socially conscious view of the world.

The movie is dense with incident: the startlingly filmed bus accident and her recovery; the couple's time in New York City where Diego is incensed when his patron, Nelson Rockefeller (Edward Norton), has the figure of Lenin removed from his mural; Frida's miscarriage; her affair with Leon Trotsky (an unconvincing Geoffrey Rush); and eventual devotion between Frida and Diego after her leg is amputated. In a touching moment at this point, Diego, though protesting he doesn't believe in God, nonetheless thanks him for having Frida in his life.

Hayek, herself a Mexican, is luminous in the role, an apt choice to play a fiery Latina. As a co-producer of the film which took years to get to the screen, it was a labor of love and a tribute to the artists of her homeland. One gets a better sense of Frida than of Diego, whose character comes across primarily as a hedonist with his own art left in the background.

Never less than visually involving, "Frida" is an audacious portrait of two flawed individuals, artists whose lives were ruled by often reckless passion.

Due to heterosexual and homosexual encounters with nudity, sporadic rough language and fleeting violence, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
